title: 🌱 Plant Growth Garden
description: Welcome to the Plant Growth Garden! You are a Grade 6 student joining the school's brand-new botany program. Over 14 weeks, you will grow plants from tiny seeds into thriving specimens — learning about germination, photosynthesis, soil science, and pollination along the way. When drought and pests strike your garden, you will need science, creativity, and teamwork to save your crops. Can you become the Master Gardener by Harvest Day?
subject: science
how_to_play: You are a Grade 6 student exploring plant science and gardening over a 14-week botany program.
Each week presents a gardening challenge with choices that affect your knowledge, plant health, and garden productivity.
Watch your dashboard — your Garden Zones (Seedling Nursery, Sunlight Lab, Soil Station, Water Systems, Harvest Plot) are interconnected.
NPCs like Ms. Bloom (teacher), Sprout (garden mascot), Priya, and Leo react to your decisions.
Random events like heatwaves and surprise rainfall will test your adaptability.
Keep Plant Health high — if it drops too low, your plants wilt and your experiments fail!
learning_objectives: Understand the stages of plant growth from seed to fruit
Explain photosynthesis and its importance to life on Earth
Identify the functions of roots, stems, leaves, and flowers
Investigate how water, sunlight, and nutrients affect plant growth
Learn about pollination and seed dispersal mechanisms
Practice the scientific method through controlled gardening experiments
cultural_context: School botany program, hands-on garden learning, sustainable agriculture awareness

behaviors.message: I am worried about your plants. They are showing serious signs of stress — yellowing leaves, drooping stems. We need to diagnose the problem: is it water, sunlight, nutrients, or something else?
You seem to be struggling with some plant science concepts. That is okay — botany can be tricky! Come see me during break and I will help you understand photosynthesis better.
Outstanding work! Your understanding of plant science is excellent and your garden is thriving. I am nominating you for the Young Botanist Award!
Your experiments are producing remarkable results and your garden designs are creative and scientifically sound. I want to feature your work at the district science showcase!
Help! The plants are thirsty! I can feel the soil drying out. Remember — plants need water for photosynthesis, nutrient transport, and keeping their cells firm. Water us please!
The soil is getting tired. Plants need nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium to grow. Without good soil, even the best seeds struggle. Time for some composting!
Look at us grow! Tall stems, green leaves, strong roots — this is what happens when you give plants the right conditions. I am the happiest sprout in the garden!
Roots happy, leaves happy, stem happy! Good soil and good water make everything possible. Keep up the excellent garden management!
Our garden is looking amazing! What if we added a sunflower maze? Or a vertical herb wall? I have so many ideas for making this the most beautiful garden in the school!
Nobody is working together! I planted seeds where Leo was supposed to set up his experiment, and nobody told me. Can we please coordinate our garden plan?
These plants are gorgeous! Strong stems, dark green leaves, and look — flower buds are forming! Our garden is going to be spectacular for Harvest Day!
Our plants are dying! The leaves are yellow and droopy. I think we are doing something wrong but I do not know what. Can someone please figure this out?
Excellent data! I have been measuring plant height every day and graphing the growth curves. Our controlled experiments are producing reliable, publishable results!
We are not recording enough data! Without proper measurements, how can we prove which conditions make plants grow best? Science needs numbers, not just guessing!

I analyzed our growth data and found something fascinating. The plants by the south wall grow 30% faster than the north wall plants — it is the sunlight angle! This proves photosynthesis is the key factor.
Our team is working like a well-oiled machine. Everyone measures, everyone records, everyone shares data. This is how real botanical research teams operate!

rounds.situation: It is your first day in the Plant Growth Garden! Ms. Bloom leads the class to the school garden plot — rows of empty raised beds, bags of soil, trays of seed packets, and shiny new tools. 'This semester, you will grow plants from seeds to harvest,' she announces. 'But this is not just gardening — it is SCIENCE. Every plant is an experiment, every leaf is data, and every flower is a result.' How do you want to start?
rounds.goal: Choose how to begin your plant science journey.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Plants take weeks to grow. Learning to wait, observe, and care for something slowly is one of life's most important skills.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does growing plants teach patience better than almost any other activity?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students arriving at a school garden with raised beds, seed packets, new tools, and bags of soil, teacher welcoming them, excited faces, sunny day

choices.label: A. Roots absorb water and minerals from soil, stems transport them upward, leaves make food through photosynthesis, and flowers help in reproduction
choices.learning_concept: Parts of a Plant and Their Functions
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Each part of a plant has a special job. Roots anchor the plant and absorb water and minerals. Stems act like highways, carrying water up to the leaves and food down from them. Leaves are the food factories — they capture sunlight and perform photosynthesis. Flowers are for reproduction — they produce seeds that grow into new plants!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Leaves absorb water from the air, and roots capture sunlight from underground
choices.learning_concept: Parts of a Plant and Their Functions
choices.feedback: You mixed them up! 💡 Roots absorb WATER and minerals from the soil (not sunlight — there is no light underground!). Leaves capture SUNLIGHT and use it for photosynthesis. Leaves do absorb carbon dioxide gas from the air, but water mainly comes in through the roots and travels up through the stem to reach the leaves.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. Flowers are just for making the plant look beautiful — they have no biological function
choices.learning_concept: Parts of a Plant and Their Functions
choices.feedback: Flowers have a crucial biological job! 💡 Flowers are the reproductive organs of a plant. They contain pollen (male) and ovules (female). Their bright colors and sweet nectar attract pollinators like bees and butterflies, which carry pollen from one flower to another. After pollination, the flower develops into a fruit containing seeds — the next generation of plants. Beauty is just a bonus!

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

choices.label: D. The stem is only for holding the plant upright — it does not transport anything inside
choices.learning_concept: Parts of a Plant and Their Functions
choices.feedback: Stems do much more than just support! 💡 If you cut a stem, you will see tiny tubes inside called xylem and phloem. Xylem tubes carry water and minerals UP from the roots to the leaves. Phloem tubes carry the food (sugar) made in the leaves DOWN to the rest of the plant. The stem is like a two-way highway for the plant's transport system!

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

rounds.situation: Ms. Bloom opens a seed and shows the tiny embryo inside: 'Every seed is a baby plant with a packed lunch! It has an embryo (the future plant), a food supply (endosperm), and a protective coat. When conditions are right — water, warmth, and oxygen — germination begins.' She challenges the class to design experiments that test what seeds need to sprout.
rounds.goal: Understand germination requirements and set up controlled seed experiments.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: A good experiment changes only ONE thing at a time. This is the most important rule in science — the controlled variable.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you planted seeds without water, would they ever germinate? What does this tell you about what seeds need?
rounds.image_prompt: Close-up of seeds sprouting in clear containers, tiny white roots emerging, student measuring with ruler, different seed types at various stages, lab setting

choices.label: A. All seeds are the same inside — the size and shape of the seed only affects how the plant looks when it grows
choices.feedback: Seeds have important internal differences! 💡 Seeds vary in the amount of stored food, number of cotyledons, and embryo structure. Monocots (like corn and wheat) have ONE cotyledon, while dicots (like beans and sunflowers) have TWO. Bigger seeds usually have more stored food, which gives the seedling a head start. A coconut seed has so much stored food that the seedling can grow for weeks before needing sunlight!

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

choices.label: B. A seed contains a tiny baby plant (embryo), stored food (cotyledon), and a protective seed coat — germination begins when it gets water, warmth, and oxygen
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A seed is like a survival kit for a baby plant! The embryo is the tiny plant waiting to grow. The cotyledon stores food (starch) to feed the embryo until it can make its own food through photosynthesis. The seed coat protects everything inside. When conditions are right — enough water, warmth, and oxygen — the seed absorbs water, swells, cracks open, and the embryo begins to grow. This process is called germination!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. A seed is not alive — it only becomes a living thing after you plant it and water it
choices.feedback: Seeds are alive — just dormant! 💡 A seed contains a living embryo that is in a resting state called dormancy. It respires (breathes) very, very slowly, using tiny amounts of stored food. Some seeds can stay dormant and alive for years — even centuries! A 2,000-year-old date palm seed found in Israel was germinated successfully. The seed is alive the whole time, just waiting for the right conditions to wake up.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. Seeds need sunlight to germinate — that is why seeds must be placed on top of the soil, not buried under it
choices.feedback: Most seeds actually germinate in the dark! 💡 Seeds buried underground can germinate perfectly well because they need water, warmth, and oxygen — NOT sunlight. The stored food in the cotyledon provides energy until the seedling pushes above the soil and reaches light. That is when sunlight becomes important — for photosynthesis. Some seeds actually germinate better in darkness!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

rounds.situation: Ms. Bloom pulls up a whole plant and lays it on the table: 'Every part has a job. Roots anchor and absorb. Stems transport and support. Leaves make food. Flowers reproduce.' She hands out plants to every team and says: 'Today, identify every part, explain its function, and discover how they all work together as a system.'
rounds.goal: Identify plant parts and understand how each contributes to the plant's survival.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: A plant is a system where every part depends on every other part. Understanding systems thinking is valuable in science and in life.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Which plant part do you think is most important? Can a plant survive without any of its parts?
rounds.image_prompt: Whole plant displayed on lab table showing roots, stem, leaves, and flower, student labeling each part with tags, magnifying glass on leaf veins, bright classroom

choices.label: A. Plants get their food by absorbing it from the soil through their roots, just like humans eat food from a plate
choices.feedback: This is one of the biggest misconceptions in science! 💡 Plants do NOT get food from the soil. Roots absorb water and dissolved minerals, but the actual FOOD (glucose) is manufactured BY THE PLANT inside its leaves through photosynthesis. Plants are producers — they MAKE their own food using sunlight, CO2, and water. If plants got food from soil, the soil would eventually disappear!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: B. Photosynthesis can happen in any part of the plant — roots, stems, and flowers all photosynthesize equally
choices.feedback: Photosynthesis mostly happens in LEAVES! 💡 Photosynthesis requires chlorophyll, the green pigment found in chloroplasts. Leaves have the most chloroplasts because they are designed to capture maximum sunlight with their flat, wide shape. Some green stems can photosynthesize too (like cactus stems), but roots (underground, no light) and flower petals (often not green) do very little or no photosynthesis.

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

choices.label: C. Photosynthesis produces carbon dioxide, which is why we should not keep plants in our bedroom at night
choices.feedback: You have it backwards! 💡 Photosynthesis takes IN carbon dioxide and releases OXYGEN — not the other way around. The equation is: CO2 + Water + Sunlight → Glucose + O2. Plants do release a tiny amount of CO2 at night during respiration (like all living things), but during the day they absorb much MORE CO2 than they release. Plants are net oxygen producers, which is why forests are called 'the lungs of the Earth'!

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. In photosynthesis, plants use sunlight energy to combine carbon dioxide (from air) and water (from soil) to make glucose (food) and release oxygen
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The photosynthesis equation is: Sunlight + Carbon Dioxide + Water → Glucose + Oxygen. This happens in chloroplasts (tiny green structures) inside leaf cells. Chlorophyll, the green pigment, captures sunlight energy. Plants absorb CO2 through tiny pores called stomata on their leaves, and water from roots. The glucose (sugar) is the plant's food, and oxygen is released as a 'waste product' that we breathe!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.round_title: Week 4: Roots & Stems — The Hidden Highway
rounds.situation: Ms. Bloom places a white carnation in a glass of blue-dyed water. 'By tomorrow, the petals will be blue,' she says. 'That is because stems have tiny tubes called xylem that carry water from roots to every leaf and flower — like a highway system inside the plant.' She challenges the class to investigate how water moves through plants and why roots are designed the way they are.
rounds.goal: Investigate root structure and water transport through stems.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: The most important work often happens underground where nobody sees it. Roots do not get credit, but they make everything above possible.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How is the xylem in a plant similar to the blood vessels in your body?
rounds.image_prompt: White carnation turning blue from dyed water, cross-section of stem showing xylem tubes, student observing with magnifying glass, colorful water experiment

choices.label: A. Plants only need water and sunlight to grow — they do not need anything from the soil or air
choices.feedback: Plants need more than just water and sunlight! 💡 Plants also need carbon dioxide from the air (absorbed through leaf stomata) as a key ingredient for photosynthesis. They also need minerals from the soil — nitrogen for making proteins and chlorophyll, phosphorus for energy transfer, and potassium for water regulation. A plant with only water and sunlight but no CO2 or minerals would be very weak and unhealthy!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: B. Adding extra water always helps plants grow faster — the more water you give, the bigger the plant gets
choices.feedback: Too much water is actually harmful! 💡 Overwatering is one of the most common ways people kill plants. When soil is waterlogged, air spaces fill with water and roots cannot get oxygen. Without oxygen, roots cannot absorb minerals and they start to rot. This condition is called root rot. Plants need the RIGHT AMOUNT of water — enough to stay hydrated but not so much that roots suffocate. Good drainage is essential!

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.

choices.label: C. Plants need four main things to grow: light (for photosynthesis), water (for transport and photosynthesis), carbon dioxide (from air), and minerals (from soil) like nitrogen and phosphorus
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Plants need light as energy for photosynthesis, water for transport and as a raw material for photosynthesis, carbon dioxide from the air for making glucose, and minerals from the soil for healthy growth. Nitrogen helps leaves grow green, phosphorus supports root and flower development, and potassium helps overall plant health. Remove any one of these, and the plant will struggle!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Plants do not need carbon dioxide — they only need oxygen, just like animals
choices.feedback: Plants need BOTH, but for different reasons! 💡 Plants need carbon dioxide for photosynthesis — it is one of the raw materials for making glucose (food). They also need oxygen for cellular respiration (breaking down glucose for energy), just like animals. During the day, plants absorb more CO2 than O2 for photosynthesis. At night, when photosynthesis stops, they only use O2 for respiration.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

rounds.situation: Ms. Bloom writes the most important equation in biology on the board: CO₂ + H₂O + Sunlight → Glucose + O₂. 'This is photosynthesis — the process that feeds nearly ALL life on Earth,' she says. 'Every leaf is a tiny food factory, using sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen. Without photosynthesis, there would be no food, no oxygen, and no life as we know it.'
rounds.goal: Understand photosynthesis and prove that plants need light to make food.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Photosynthesis connects sunlight, air, water, and soil into one amazing process. Understanding this equation unlocks the secret of all life on Earth.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If plants produce the oxygen we breathe, what responsibility do we have to protect forests and green spaces?
rounds.image_prompt: Leaf cross-section diagram showing chloroplasts absorbing light, CO2 and H2O entering, glucose and O2 being produced, student comparing leaf colors in sunlight

choices.label: A. Plants lose water through their roots, not their leaves, because roots are in contact with wet soil
choices.feedback: It is the opposite! 💡 Roots ABSORB water; leaves LOSE water. Leaves have thousands of tiny pores called stomata (a single leaf can have 100,000+ stomata!) through which water vapor escapes into the air. This is transpiration. You can prove it: put a plastic bag over a plant's leaves and you will see water droplets collect inside the bag. Roots take water in; leaves let water out!

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

choices.label: B. Transpiration is just another word for photosynthesis — they are the same process
choices.feedback: They are completely different processes! 💡 Photosynthesis is making FOOD (glucose) using sunlight, CO2, and water. Transpiration is the LOSS of water vapor through stomata on leaves. However, they are connected — stomata open to let CO2 in for photosynthesis, but water escapes at the same time (transpiration). About 99% of water absorbed by roots is lost through transpiration — only 1% is used for photosynthesis!

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: C. Water moves up a plant because the roots push it upward with strong pumping pressure, like a heart
choices.feedback: Plants do not have pumps like hearts! 💡 While roots do create a small amount of 'root pressure,' the main force pulling water up the plant is TRANSPIRATION — evaporation from the leaves. As water molecules evaporate from stomata, they pull the water molecules below them upward (because water molecules stick together — this is called cohesion). It is a pulling force from the top, not a pushing force from the bottom!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: D. Transpiration is the process where water evaporates from tiny pores (stomata) on leaves, pulling more water up from the roots through the stem like a chain
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Transpiration is like a natural water pump! As water evaporates from stomata on the leaf surface, it creates a 'pull' that draws water up through the xylem tubes in the stem, all the way from the roots. This is called the transpiration stream. A sunflower can pull up over 1 liter of water per day! Transpiration also cools the plant, similar to how sweating cools humans.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: Ms. Bloom explains: 'Water and minerals are the other half of the plant growth equation. Plants need nitrogen for leaves, phosphorus for roots and flowers, and potassium for overall health. Too little nutrients and plants starve. Too much and you can burn the roots!' She brings out fertilizer samples and testing kits. Leo is already planning experiments.
rounds.goal: Understand the role of water and mineral nutrients in plant growth.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Using fertilizers responsibly matters — over-fertilizing pollutes waterways and harms ecosystems. Sustainable gardening means using only what plants need.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If fertilizer helps plants grow, why can too much fertilizer be harmful — both to the plant and to the environment?
rounds.image_prompt: Students testing soil nutrients with color-coded test kit, bags of organic fertilizer, watering cans, comparison of healthy vs nutrient-deficient plants side by side

choices.label: A. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther (male part) to the stigma (female part) of a flower, often carried by insects, wind, or birds
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Pollination is how flowering plants reproduce. The anther (on the stamen) produces pollen grains. These must reach the stigma (on the pistil) of the same or another flower. Bees are champion pollinators — they visit flowers for nectar and pollen sticks to their fuzzy bodies. Wind pollinates grasses and many trees. After pollen reaches the stigma, it grows a tube down to the ovule for fertilization!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Pollination is when seeds are scattered to new places by wind or animals
choices.feedback: That describes seed dispersal, not pollination! 💡 Pollination and seed dispersal are two different stages. POLLINATION comes first — it is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma, leading to fertilization and seed formation. SEED DISPERSAL comes later — it is spreading the seeds to new locations. First pollen travels (pollination), then seeds travel (dispersal). Do not mix them up!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. All flowers are pollinated by bees — plants that do not attract bees cannot reproduce
choices.feedback: There are many types of pollinators! 💡 While bees are important pollinators, flowers can also be pollinated by butterflies, moths, bats, hummingbirds, and even water! Many plants (like grasses, wheat, and many trees) are pollinated by WIND — they produce huge amounts of light, dusty pollen that floats through the air. Wind-pollinated flowers are usually small and plain because they do not need to attract insects.

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: D. Flowers are brightly colored just to look pretty — the color has nothing to do with pollination
choices.feedback: Flower colors have an important purpose! 💡 Bright colors, sweet scents, and nectar are all adaptations to ATTRACT pollinators. Red flowers attract hummingbirds, blue and purple flowers attract bees, and white flowers that bloom at night attract moths. Each flower has evolved colors and patterns to attract its specific pollinator. Some flowers even have ultraviolet patterns visible only to bees, guiding them to the nectar like runway lights!

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! A record heatwave hits the area. Temperatures soar above 40°C for a full week, the school's water supply is restricted to essential use only, and the garden bakes in relentless sun. Your precious seedlings are wilting, leaves are curling, and the soil is cracking. Ms. Bloom is concerned: 'This is a real challenge. Plants need water to survive — and we have almost none. How do we save our garden?'
rounds.goal: Save your garden during a severe drought with limited water resources.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Adversity reveals resourcefulness. When water is scarce, you discover how much creativity and teamwork matter. The best farmers are the ones who survive the worst droughts.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How do farmers in dry regions like Rajasthan manage to grow crops with very little water? What can we learn from them?
rounds.image_prompt: School garden in a heatwave, cracked dry soil, wilting plants, students carefully rationing water from small containers, shade cloth being set up, intense sun

choices.label: A. Seeds are dispersed (spread) by wind (dandelions), animals (berries eaten by birds), water (coconuts floating), and explosion (pea pods popping open)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Plants have amazing ways to spread their seeds! Wind dispersal: dandelion fluff and maple 'helicopters' float through the air. Animal dispersal: birds eat berries and deposit seeds in droppings far away; burrs stick to animal fur. Water dispersal: coconuts float across oceans. Explosive dispersal: some seed pods dry out and burst open, flinging seeds meters away! Dispersal prevents overcrowding and helps plants colonize new areas.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Fruits exist only so that humans can eat them — they have no role in seed dispersal
choices.feedback: Fruits evolved FOR seed dispersal! 💡 Fruits are the plant's clever trick to get animals to carry seeds away. Animals eat the sweet, nutritious fruit and the seeds pass through their digestive system unharmed, getting deposited far from the parent plant — complete with a dollop of fertilizer (animal droppings)! Humans are just one of many animals that help disperse seeds by eating fruit. The plant 'pays' us with tasty fruit in exchange for seed transport!

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: C. Wind can only disperse very large, heavy seeds because small seeds are too light to be carried
choices.feedback: It is the exact opposite! 💡 Wind disperses SMALL, LIGHT seeds — not heavy ones. Dandelion seeds have fluffy parachutes, maple seeds have paper-thin wings, and orchid seeds are microscopic dust-like particles. These adaptations help them catch the wind and float far away. Heavy seeds like coconuts are dispersed by WATER (floating), and medium seeds in fruits are dispersed by ANIMALS. Light + wings or fluff = wind dispersal!

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

choices.label: D. All seeds simply fall directly below the parent plant — they do not travel to new places
choices.feedback: Seeds travel amazing distances! 💡 If all seeds fell directly below the parent plant, they would compete with the parent and each other for light, water, and nutrients. That is why plants have evolved clever dispersal methods. Dandelion seeds can travel kilometers on the wind. Coconuts float across entire oceans. Birds can carry seeds hundreds of kilometers. Some orchid seeds are so tiny they drift like dust on air currents!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

rounds.situation: The drought is over, rain has returned, and — miracle of miracles — the first flowers are blooming! Ms. Bloom is delighted: 'Flowers are not just pretty decorations. They are the reproductive organs of a plant. Each flower is designed to attract pollinators — bees, butterflies, birds — who carry pollen from one flower to another. This is how plants make seeds!' The garden is buzzing with insect visitors.
rounds.goal: Understand flower structure and the process of pollination.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: Plants and pollinators need each other. This mutual dependence — called mutualism — is one of nature's most beautiful partnerships.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If all the bees disappeared tomorrow, what would happen to our food supply? Why are pollinators so important?
rounds.image_prompt: Colorful flowers in school garden with bees and butterflies visiting, student using magnifying glass to examine pollen on flower parts, bright and vibrant scene

choices.label: A. Phototropism is when a plant grows TOWARD light, and geotropism (gravitropism) is when roots grow DOWNWARD toward gravity — these help plants find sunlight and water
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Tropisms are growth responses to stimuli. Phototropism: shoots grow toward light to maximize photosynthesis (controlled by the hormone auxin, which causes cells on the dark side to grow longer, bending the stem toward light). Geotropism: roots grow downward following gravity to find water and anchor the plant, while shoots grow upward against gravity. There is also hydrotropism — roots growing toward water!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. Phototropism means plants grow toward water, because 'photo' means water in Greek
choices.feedback: Check the word origins! 💡 'Photo' means LIGHT in Greek (think 'photograph' = writing with light). So phototropism = growth toward LIGHT. Growing toward water is called HYDROTROPISM ('hydro' = water). And growing in response to gravity is called GEOTROPISM or gravitropism ('geo' = earth). Knowing these Greek roots helps: photo = light, hydro = water, geo = earth, thigmo = touch!

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

choices.label: C. Roots grow toward light and shoots grow away from light, because roots need sunlight to absorb water
choices.feedback: You have it reversed! 💡 SHOOTS grow TOWARD light (positive phototropism) because leaves need sunlight for photosynthesis. ROOTS grow AWAY from light (negative phototropism) and TOWARD gravity (positive geotropism) because they need to go deeper into soil to find water and minerals. Roots do not need sunlight — they absorb water, which is underground. Each part grows in the direction that helps it do its job!

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. Plants cannot sense or respond to anything in their environment — they grow in completely random directions
choices.feedback: Plants are surprisingly responsive! 💡 Even though plants cannot move around like animals, they can sense light, gravity, water, and touch, and they grow in response. Put a plant in a window and watch its stems bend toward the light within days — that is phototropism. Turn a potted plant sideways and the roots will reorient downward — that is geotropism. Plants use hormones like auxin to control these growth responses.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

rounds.round_title: Week 9: Fruits & Seeds — The Next Generation
rounds.situation: The pollinated flowers are transforming! Petals fall away and fruits begin to swell — tiny green tomatoes, bean pods lengthening, and sunflower heads filling with seeds. Ms. Bloom explains: 'A fruit is a ripened ovary that protects seeds. Each seed is a new potential plant. But seeds need to travel AWAY from the parent plant — this is seed dispersal.' She asks: 'How many ways can a seed travel?'
rounds.goal: Understand fruit development and the mechanisms of seed dispersal.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Nature invented hundreds of ways to move seeds — wind, water, animals, explosions. Studying these methods reveals nature's incredible engineering creativity.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If all seeds just fell straight down under the parent plant, what problems would that cause?
rounds.image_prompt: Various fruits and seeds displayed — dandelion puffs, burrs on socks, berries, maple seeds, bean pods bursting open, students examining and sorting them

choices.label: A. Plants get all their nutrients from sunlight and air — soil just holds the plant in place and provides water
choices.feedback: Soil provides essential minerals! 💡 While plants DO get carbon from CO2 in the air and energy from sunlight, they need at least 16 mineral nutrients from the soil, including nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, and iron. Without these, plants become yellow, weak, and stunted. This is why farmers test their soil and add fertilizers — to replace minerals that crops have used up!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: B. Plants with yellow leaves just need more water — leaf color is only affected by watering, not nutrients
choices.feedback: Yellow leaves often signal nutrient deficiency! 💡 When leaves turn yellow (chlorosis), it is frequently because the plant lacks nitrogen — the key ingredient for making chlorophyll (the green pigment). Without enough nitrogen, plants cannot make chlorophyll, so leaves lose their green color. Purple leaves can indicate phosphorus deficiency, and brown leaf edges can mean potassium deficiency. Leaf color is a plant's way of telling you what it needs!

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.

choices.label: C. Any type of soil works equally well for growing plants — soil quality does not matter
choices.feedback: Soil quality matters enormously! 💡 Different soils have different nutrient levels, drainage, and pH (acidity). Sandy soil drains too fast and loses nutrients. Clay soil holds too much water and can suffocate roots. Loamy soil (a mix of sand, silt, and clay) is ideal — it holds nutrients and water while still allowing air to reach roots. Adding compost improves soil by adding nutrients, improving drainage, and feeding beneficial soil organisms!

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. Plants need three main soil nutrients: nitrogen (N) for leaf growth, phosphorus (P) for roots and flowers, and potassium (K) for overall health — these are called NPK
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ NPK are the 'big three' nutrients that plants need most. Nitrogen (N) helps leaves grow green and lush — it is needed for making chlorophyll and proteins. Phosphorus (P) supports strong root development and flower/fruit production. Potassium (K) helps with overall plant health, disease resistance, and water regulation. That is why fertilizer bags always show three numbers (like 10-10-10) representing N-P-K ratios!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Ms. Bloom announces: 'You have learned about every factor that affects plant growth — light, water, soil, nutrients, and temperature. Now it is time to put it all together. Design the PERFECT growing conditions for a plant of your choice. Optimize everything and grow the biggest, healthiest specimen you can. This is applied botany!'
rounds.goal: Apply all your plant science knowledge to optimize growing conditions for maximum growth.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Optimization means balancing all factors at once. Too much of anything — even good things like water or fertilizer — can hurt. Balance is the key.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is balance so important in plant growth? Can a plant have too much of a good thing?
rounds.image_prompt: Student carefully measuring and adjusting growing conditions — sunlight meter, soil moisture probe, fertilizer bottle — next to thriving plants, organized workspace

choices.label: A. Non-flowering plants cannot reproduce — only flowering plants can make new plants
choices.feedback: Non-flowering plants reproduce very successfully! 💡 Ferns produce millions of tiny spores on the undersides of their leaves (look for brown dots called sori). These spores float through the air and grow into new ferns. Mosses also use spores. Conifers produce seeds inside cones — pine nuts are actually conifer seeds! Non-flowering plants have thrived for hundreds of millions of years using these methods.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: B. Ferns and mosses are not real plants because they do not have flowers or produce seeds
choices.feedback: Ferns and mosses are absolutely real plants! 💡 They are green, they photosynthesize, and they have been on Earth much longer than flowering plants! Ferns have roots, stems, and leaves (called fronds) and can grow very large. They just reproduce differently — using spores instead of seeds. Plants are classified by their characteristics (photosynthesis, cell walls, etc.), not by whether they have flowers. Flowers are just one strategy!

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

choices.label: C. Flowering plants (angiosperms) reproduce using flowers and fruits, while non-flowering plants like ferns use spores and conifers use cones instead of flowers
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The plant kingdom has two main groups based on reproduction. Flowering plants (angiosperms) are the largest group — roses, mango trees, grasses, and most food crops. They produce flowers, fruits, and seeds. Non-flowering plants include ferns (reproduce with spores — tiny dust-like cells), mosses (also spores), and conifers like pine trees (reproduce using cones, not flowers). Each group has evolved its own amazing way to reproduce!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. All plants produce flowers — some flowers are just too small to see with the naked eye
choices.feedback: Many plants never produce flowers at all! 💡 Ferns, mosses, horsetails, and liverworts are completely non-flowering plants — they reproduce using tiny cells called spores instead. Conifers (pine, cedar, spruce) are also non-flowering — they use cones. Pine trees have been around for over 300 million years, long before flowers evolved! Flowering plants only appeared about 130 million years ago. Non-flowering plants are actually more ancient!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

rounds.situation: Ms. Bloom digs into the garden bed and pulls out a handful of rich, dark soil: 'This is not just dirt — it is alive! One teaspoon of healthy soil contains more microorganisms than there are people on Earth. Soil is a complex ecosystem of minerals, organic matter, water, air, and billions of living things. Today we go deep — literally — into soil science.'
rounds.goal: Investigate soil composition, soil types, and the soil ecosystem.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: The most important things are often the least visible. Soil is the foundation of all land-based life, yet most people never think about it. Appreciate the invisible foundations.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How is healthy soil similar to a healthy community? What happens when the foundation is neglected?
rounds.image_prompt: Students examining layers of soil in a clear container, visible earthworms and root structures, soil pH testing, hand holding rich dark compost, outdoor setting

choices.label: A. Earthworms damage soil by eating the nutrients that plants need and creating holes that cause erosion
choices.feedback: Earthworms are soil superheroes! 💡 Their tunnels actually IMPROVE soil by creating air passages and water channels for plant roots. Earthworm castings (their waste) are one of the richest natural fertilizers — packed with nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. They also mix and churn soil layers, pulling dead leaves underground where bacteria can decompose them faster. A healthy garden soil might have 1 million earthworms per acre!

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: B. Soil is made of layers: topsoil (dark, nutrient-rich, where most roots grow), subsoil (lighter, with minerals), and bedrock (solid rock beneath) — earthworms and bacteria make topsoil fertile
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Soil has distinct layers called horizons. The topsoil (A horizon) is the dark, crumbly layer where most plant roots, earthworms, and microorganisms live. It is rich in humus (decomposed organic matter). Below is the subsoil (B horizon), which has fewer organisms but contains minerals washed down from above. Below that is the parent rock (C horizon) and solid bedrock. It takes about 500 years to form just 2.5 cm of topsoil!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. Soil is the same from the surface all the way down to the center of the Earth — it does not have different layers
choices.feedback: Soil has very distinct layers! 💡 If you dig a deep hole, you can clearly see different layers (called horizons). The top layer is dark brown or black — that is topsoil, rich with decomposed leaves and organisms. Below is lighter-colored subsoil with fewer nutrients. Then comes partially broken rock, and finally solid bedrock. Each layer looks different and has different properties. Scientists who study soil (pedologists) can read these layers like pages of a book!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: D. Composting is useless because the nutrients in dead leaves are destroyed when the leaves decompose
choices.feedback: Composting is incredibly valuable! 💡 When dead leaves and food scraps decompose, nutrients are NOT destroyed — they are RELEASED back into simpler forms that plants can absorb. Decomposition by bacteria and fungi breaks complex organic molecules into simple minerals like nitrogen and phosphorus compounds. Compost also improves soil structure, helps soil hold water, and feeds beneficial organisms. Composting is nature's ultimate recycling program!

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! When you check the garden on Monday morning, disaster has struck. Aphids — tiny green insects — cover every tomato plant. Caterpillars are munching through the lettuce. And something has been digging up the carrot bed overnight! Ms. Bloom looks at the damage and says: 'This is a pest outbreak. If we do not act fast, we could lose the entire harvest. But remember — every pest is also a living organism with a role in the ecosystem. How we respond matters.'
rounds.goal: Manage a garden pest outbreak using science-based, responsible methods.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: The easiest solution (chemical pesticides) often causes the most long-term harm. Sustainable pest management requires thinking about the whole ecosystem.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why might chemical pesticides solve the immediate problem but create bigger problems in the long run?
rounds.image_prompt: School garden with visible aphids on tomato plants, caterpillar-eaten lettuce, concerned students examining damage with magnifying glasses, ladybug on a leaf nearby

choices.label: A. Plants cannot defend themselves against pests at all — they just have to wait and hope the pests go away
choices.feedback: Plants are surprisingly good at defense! 💡 Even though plants cannot run away, they have evolved many defenses over millions of years. Roses have thorns, cacti have spines, poison ivy produces oils that cause itchy rashes, and chili peppers produce capsaicin that burns mouths. Some acacia trees even release chemicals into the air that warn nearby trees to start producing defensive chemicals before the pests reach them. Plants communicate and fight back!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: B. Insects are always harmful to plants — a garden with zero insects would be the healthiest garden
choices.feedback: Many insects are essential for healthy gardens! 💡 Bees and butterflies are vital pollinators — without them, many plants cannot produce fruit or seeds. Ladybugs eat aphids (plant pests). Earthworms aerate soil. Dragonflies eat mosquitoes. Only about 3% of insect species are considered crop pests! A garden without any insects would actually fail because flowers would not get pollinated and soil would become poor quality.

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

choices.label: C. Plants defend themselves against pests using thorns, tough bark, bad-tasting chemicals, and even releasing scents that attract the predators of the pests attacking them
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Plants have amazing defense systems! Physical defenses include thorns (roses), thick bark (trees), waxy coatings, and stinging hairs (nettles). Chemical defenses include bitter or toxic compounds — caffeine in coffee plants and nicotine in tobacco are natural pesticides! Some plants are even cleverer: when caterpillars attack, they release chemicals that attract wasps that eat the caterpillars. It is like calling for backup!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Using lots of chemical pesticides is always the best way to protect plants, with no negative effects on the ecosystem
choices.feedback: Chemical pesticides have serious downsides! 💡 While pesticides kill target pests, they also kill beneficial insects like bees (essential pollinators) and ladybugs (which eat aphids). Pesticides wash into rivers and poison fish. Pests can develop resistance, requiring stronger chemicals. Organic methods like companion planting (growing marigolds to repel insects), introducing natural predators (ladybugs), and crop rotation are safer, sustainable alternatives!

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Considering fairness in your decision demonstrates ethical thinking.

rounds.situation: One week before Harvest Day! Ms. Bloom gives the class full creative freedom: 'Design and build the most innovative garden feature you can imagine. Use everything you have learned — soil science, photosynthesis, water management, pollination. Think vertical, think sustainable, think beautiful. Show the world what plant science can do!' Priya is already sketching wild designs.
rounds.goal: Apply all your botany knowledge to create an innovative garden project.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Innovation happens when you combine knowledge from different areas in new ways. Every great garden started as an idea in someone's imagination.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How does understanding the science of plants make you a BETTER gardener, not just a more knowledgeable one?
rounds.image_prompt: Students building creative garden projects — vertical pallet garden, hanging herb tower, recycled bottle planters, artistic garden features, active and excited

choices.label: A. When you plant a seed, the new plant is an exact copy (clone) of the parent plant with identical genes
choices.learning_concept: Sexual and Asexual Reproduction in Plants
choices.feedback: Seeds produce genetically unique plants! 💡 Seeds are formed through sexual reproduction — pollen from one plant fertilizes the ovule of another (or the same) plant, combining genes from both parents. The resulting seed has a unique mix of genes, just like human siblings are different from each other. Only asexual reproduction (cuttings, runners, tubers) produces exact genetic clones. This genetic mixing is why seed-grown plants show variety!

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

choices.label: B. Asexual reproduction in plants always produces stronger, healthier plants than sexual reproduction
choices.learning_concept: Sexual and Asexual Reproduction in Plants
choices.feedback: Both methods have pros and cons! 💡 Asexual reproduction is fast and reliable — but all offspring are genetic clones, so if a disease affects one, it affects ALL of them (the Irish Potato Famine happened because all potatoes were clones of the same variety). Sexual reproduction through seeds is slower but creates genetic diversity — different offspring have different traits, so some will survive even if conditions change or diseases strike.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: C. Plants can only reproduce from seeds — there is no other way for a plant to create a new plant
choices.learning_concept: Sexual and Asexual Reproduction in Plants
choices.feedback: Plants have many ways to reproduce without seeds! 💡 This is called vegetative or asexual reproduction. You can grow a new plant from a potato 'eye' (tuber), a strawberry runner, a garlic clove (bulb), or even a stem cutting placed in water. Bananas, many roses, and most potatoes are grown this way. The new plant is a genetic clone of the parent. Gardeners use this to copy their best plants exactly!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: D. Plants can reproduce sexually (through seeds formed after pollination) or asexually (through runners, bulbs, tubers, or cuttings — creating clones of the parent)
choices.learning_concept: Sexual and Asexual Reproduction in Plants
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Sexual reproduction involves pollen and ovules combining to form seeds with mixed genes from two parents — creating variety that helps species adapt. Asexual (vegetative) reproduction creates genetically identical clones: strawberry runners creep along the ground and grow new plants, potato tubers sprout new plants, and gardeners can grow new plants from stem cuttings. Each method has advantages!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Harvest Day is here! The garden is overflowing with ripe vegetables, fragrant herbs, and colorful flowers. Parents, teachers, younger students, and a local chef are visiting. Ms. Bloom says: 'This is your moment. 14 weeks ago you planted tiny seeds. Today you are harvesting knowledge, food, and memories. Show everyone what plant science can do!' How will you present your work?
rounds.goal: Present your plant science knowledge and garden achievements at the harvest showcase.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: From seeds to harvest, you watched life unfold through patience, science, and care. This is what delayed gratification looks like in its most beautiful form.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at Week 1, what would you tell your past self about growing plants? What was the most surprising thing you learned?
rounds.image_prompt: School Harvest Day, students displaying vegetables and herbs, parents visiting garden, colorful flowers, project posters, chef examining produce, proud joyful atmosphere

choices.label: A. Plants are less important than animals because animals are at the top of the food chain and control the ecosystem
choices.learning_concept: Plants as the Foundation of Life
choices.feedback: Plants are MORE important than many people realize! 💡 Without plants, all food chains would collapse because plants are the only organisms that can convert sunlight into food. Remove all animals, and plants would still survive. Remove all plants, and almost all animals would die. Plants also produce the oxygen we breathe, regulate climate by absorbing CO2, prevent soil erosion, and purify water. Animals depend on plants, not the other way around!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: B. We do not need to protect forests because we can easily replace plants with artificial food-making machines
choices.learning_concept: Plants as the Foundation of Life
choices.feedback: We cannot replace what plants do! 💡 No human technology can match what plants do naturally. A single tree can absorb 22 kg of CO2 per year, release enough oxygen for 2 people, filter water, prevent erosion, provide habitat for hundreds of species, cool the air, and produce food — all powered by free sunlight! Forests also regulate rainfall patterns and store carbon that would otherwise warm our planet. Protecting forests is protecting our future!

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.

choices.label: C. Plants are the foundation of almost all food chains because they are producers — they convert sunlight into chemical energy (glucose) that feeds nearly all other life on Earth
choices.learning_concept: Plants as the Foundation of Life
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Plants are the ultimate producers of our planet. Through photosynthesis, they capture the sun's energy and store it as glucose. This energy then flows through the entire food chain — herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat herbivores. Without plants, there would be no food for animals and no oxygen to breathe. Plants also provide materials for shelter, clothing, and medicine. They truly are the foundation of life on Earth!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Weighing the ethical implications shows principled reasoning.

choices.label: D. Photosynthesis only matters for the plant itself — the oxygen released is just waste and is not important for other organisms
choices.learning_concept: Plants as the Foundation of Life
choices.feedback: Oxygen from photosynthesis is essential for life! 💡 The 'waste' oxygen from photosynthesis is what almost all animals (including humans) breathe. Before plants evolved photosynthesis billions of years ago, Earth's atmosphere had almost no oxygen, and complex animal life could not exist. Plants produce about 50% of Earth's oxygen (the other 50% comes from ocean algae and phytoplankton, which also photosynthesize). That oxygen 'waste' is our lifeline!

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which plants use sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water to make glucose (food) and release oxygen. The equation: CO₂ + H₂O + Sunlight → Glucose + O₂.
The process by which a seed begins to grow into a new plant. It requires water, warmth, and oxygen — but not light.
The green pigment in plant leaves that captures sunlight energy for photosynthesis. It absorbs red and blue light but reflects green — which is why leaves look green.
Tube-like structures inside plant stems that transport water and dissolved minerals upward from roots to leaves, driven by transpiration pull.
Tube-like structures inside plant stems that transport sugars (food made by photosynthesis) from leaves to all other parts of the plant.
The loss of water vapor through tiny pores (stomata) in plant leaves. This process pulls water up from the roots and helps cool the plant.
The transfer of pollen from the male part (stamen) to the female part (pistil) of a flower, usually carried by insects, birds, or wind. Essential for seed and fruit production.
The methods by which seeds are spread away from the parent plant — by wind (dandelion), water (coconut), animals (burrs), or explosion (balsam pod).
The three main minerals plants need: Nitrogen (N) for leaf growth, Phosphorus (P) for root and flower development, and Potassium (K) for overall health and disease resistance.
Decomposed organic matter (food scraps, leaves, manure) that enriches soil with nutrients and improves its structure. Nature's recycling system.
Tiny pores on the underside of leaves that open and close to allow gas exchange — CO₂ in for photosynthesis, O₂ and water vapor out.
Growing certain plants together because they benefit each other — for example, basil repels aphids from tomatoes, and beans add nitrogen that corn needs.

endings.title: Master Botanist
endings.message: You have achieved mastery in the Plant Growth Garden! Your botany knowledge is extraordinary, your garden is a showcase of health and creativity, and your experiments produced real scientific insights. Ms. Bloom nominates you for the Young Botanist Award, and the visiting chef wants to feature your garden vegetables in a local restaurant menu. You have proven that patience, science, and care can transform tiny seeds into something magnificent!

endings.title: Skilled Gardener
endings.message: You have become a skilled gardener with solid plant science knowledge! Your Harvest Day display shows real understanding of plant biology and good growing practices. Ms. Bloom says you are ready for the advanced biology elective next year. Your green thumb and scientific mind are a powerful combination!

endings.title: Garden Regular
endings.message: You completed the Plant Growth Garden program with growing confidence. Some weeks were tough — the drought and the pest invasion tested everyone — but you stuck with it and learned the fundamentals of plant science. Ms. Bloom says there is always next season to improve. Keep growing — every expert gardener started with their first seed!

endings.title: Struggling Grower
endings.message: The Plant Growth Garden was a challenging journey for you. Many plants wilted and experiments did not always work out. But here is the important thing — you kept trying. Ms. Bloom arranges extra practice sessions and says: 'Even professional gardeners lose plants. What matters is learning why and trying again.' Your gardening story is just beginning!

endings.title: Garden in Trouble
endings.message: The garden has suffered significant losses this semester. Many plants did not survive the drought and pest invasion, and the soil needs serious restoration. It is a hard lesson, but Ms. Bloom reminds you: 'Every great garden was once bare soil. What matters is that you learned from this experience. Next semester, we will start fresh with the knowledge you gained.' Sprout gives you a hug.
